articles.title: Version control with Git: never lose work again
articles.summary: Why version control exists, how local, centralised and distributed systems differ, and the everyday Git workflow: stage, commit, branch, merge and share.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Every project eventually produces project_v1.py, project_v2_final.py and Report_2024_FINAL_FINAL.docx, plus working, working_3 and old/new folders nobody dares delete. Undo buffers only cover the last few edits in one file, collaborators overwrite each other, and nobody can answer who changed what, when, or why. A version control system (VCS) fixes all of this: it records every change to a project with who made it, when, and a message saying why, so any version can be inspected, compared and restored.

Git is the dominant VCS, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for Linux kernel development. Git is not GitHub: Git is the tool on your machine, while GitHub (like GitLab and Bitbucket) is a hosting service that adds remote storage, issue tracking and code review around it.

sections.heading: Three architectures
paras: A local VCS keeps the version database on one computer (for example RCS deltas or File History): simple, but useless for teams. A centralised VCS (CVCS) keeps one central server that everyone checks out from and checks in to, with file locking; administration is easy but the server is a single point of failure. A distributed VCS (DVCS) like Git or Mercurial gives every user a full copy of the history, so you can commit offline and there is no single point of failure, at the cost of needing workflow discipline.

head: System
Where history lives
Strength
Weakness
rows: Offline work, no single failure point

sections.heading: The four places and file states
paras: Git work flows through four locations: your working directory (the files you edit), the staging area (a preparation zone for the next commit), the local repository (committed snapshots in .git), and the remote repository (the shared copy on a server). The cycle is checkout, edit, add (stage), commit (snapshot locally), push (share) and pull (collect others' work). A bare repository holds only history with no working directory and serves as a collaboration hub nobody edits directly.

Files move through states you can read in git status: untracked files Git ignores until added; tracked files that are unmodified, modified, or staged. git add moves changes into staging, git commit snapshots staging into history, git reset unstages, and git checkout -- or git restore discards working-directory edits.

sections.heading: Everyday commands
paras: Setup is once per machine: install Git, then git config --global user.name and user.email so every commit carries your identity. Per project: git init to start, or git clone to copy an existing remote. Then the loop: edit, git add the files, git commit -m with a message describing one logical change, and inspect with git log --graph, git diff and git status. Compare any two commits with git diff <hash1> <hash2>, where added lines show with + and removed with -.

Branching keeps unfinished work off the main line: git branch my-new-branch then git switch to it (or the combined git switch -c / git checkout -b), commit normally, and git switch master plus git merge to bring it back. Never commit directly on master or main for team work; push the branch, open a pull request, have a teammate review, merge, and let everyone pull. Merge commits carry both histories; when both sides edited the same lines Git reports a conflict for a human to resolve.
bullets: One logical change per commit, with a message that explains why.
Commit before switching branches so work is never stranded.
Never work directly on master/main in a team; review before merging.
Clone once, then pull regularly; push and pull never overwrite history.

sections.heading: Team workflow and traceability
paras: The standard team loop is: clone once, create a feature branch, commit in small logical steps, push the branch, request review, merge to master after approval, and pull master to stay current. Because commits are immutable, history doubles as documentation: git log shows who changed what and when, and git checkout of an old hash restores any past version for debugging. If every commit message explains its reason, future-you (and your teammates) can trace any bug to the decision that introduced it.

callout.text: If asked to sketch a workflow, draw the four places with the six arrows (checkout/add/commit/push/pull/clone) and state the branch rule: feature branch, pull request, review, merge to main, never commit on main directly.

recall.q: What do the staging area and a commit each do?
recall.a: The staging area (git add) prepares exactly what the next snapshot will contain; a commit (git commit) permanently records that snapshot in the local repository with author, date and message.

recall.q: How do LVCS, CVCS and DVCS differ?
recall.a: LVCS keeps history on one machine (no collaboration); CVCS keeps one central server (easy admin, single point of failure); DVCS gives every clone full history (offline commits, no single failure, needs discipline). Git is distributed.

recall.q: What is the safe team branching workflow?
recall.a: Branch off main for each feature, commit small logical steps, push the branch, open a pull request, merge only after review, then everyone pulls. Never commit directly on main.

citations.excerpt: A version control system records every change with who, when and why so any version can be restored. Local systems keep history on one computer, centralised systems on one server with file locking, distributed systems give every user a full copy.

citations.excerpt: Work flows through working directory, staging area, local repository and remote repository via checkout, add, commit, push and pull. Files are untracked or tracked (unmodified, modified, staged); git add stages, git commit snapshots, git status and git diff inspect.

articles.title: Modularity: coupling, cohesion and reuse
articles.summary: Decompose systems into independent, single-job modules: high cohesion, low coupling, no globals or control flags, and reuse without duplication.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Software design sits between requirements and code, and its central idea is modularity: building self-contained functions, classes and modules that each do one job well, like prefabricated walls, windows and beams in construction. You should be able to use a module without knowing how it is made, test and change it in isolation, and compose it with others into larger behaviour.

Four principles guide the design: high cohesion (everything inside a module belongs together), low coupling (modules depend on each other as little as possible), information hiding (expose only what callers need), and code reuse. Two of Lehman's laws explain why this matters: continuing change means a useful program must keep evolving, and increasing complexity means every change makes the system messier unless you actively clean it up through refactoring, which is behaviour-preserving cleanup such as splitting, combining or rewiring modules.

sections.heading: Maintenance never ends
paras: Maintenance begins the day software is delivered, and unlike hardware, software does not wear out: every future failure is a bug that was always there, surfacing when a new input or environment finally triggers it. Corrective maintenance fixes small defects, perfective maintenance adds or improves features, and adaptive maintenance ports the system to new environments. Modularity decides how painful each kind is: a well-decomposed system localises most changes to one module.

sections.heading: Coupling: how modules depend on each other
paras: Coupling measures dependence between modules. Some coupling is essential: calcDaysInMonth calling isLeapYear(y) is a normal parameterised call where the caller pauses, passes y, and resumes with the answer. Trouble starts with hidden or excessive coupling.

Global variables are the classic hidden coupling: any module can read or change them at any time, so a fault could originate anywhere and tracing it means reading everything. The fix is boring on purpose: pass data in as parameters and return results, so each call is self-contained. A second smell is the long parameter list (more than about six): a function taking unit, code, building, room, capacity and more is probably doing several jobs and should be split. A third is the control flag: formatTimeDate(day, month, year, isDate) behaves as two different functions depending on a Boolean, forcing callers to know its internals. Split it into formatDate plus formatTime and the flag (and the extra coupling) disappears.

head: Smell
Why it hurts
Fix
rows: Any module can change them; faults untraceable
Module does several jobs; callers carry context
One function, two behaviours; caller knows internals

sections.heading: Cohesion: what belongs together
paras: Cohesion measures focus within a module. calculate_tax is cohesive; calculate_tax_and_send_email is not, because tax logic and email logic change for unrelated reasons. Practise spotting the split: process_data doing clean, save and notify is three sequential tasks that should become three functions; checkAgeAndPostcode validating two unrelated ranges should become checkAge plus checkPostcode so each half is reusable alone. Relatedness runs from unrelated (split immediately) through related-by-name or by time, up to related-by-data, which is often tightly coupled and deserves a second look. Fixing coupling usually improves cohesion at the same time, and vice versa.

sections.heading: Reuse without duplication
paras: Duplication is the hardware-software inversion students forget: redundant fans make hardware more reliable, but duplicated code makes software worse, because every copy must be tested and every fix applied everywhere. Consolidate instead: if two fragments match, keep one; if one extends the other, extract the shared part; if several share a core, extract it as a helper like calcXY reused by both printSpecial and getNM. But reuse increases coupling, so only reuse genuinely identical tasks: never force it, never mistake similar for same, and never let reuse wreck cohesion.

callout.text: Given a code smell, name it (global, long params, control flag, low cohesion, duplication), explain the coupling/cohesion harm in one sentence, and show the refactored version. Marks split evenly across the three moves.

recall.q: What are the four modularity principles and what do they buy you?
recall.a: High cohesion, low coupling, information hiding, code reuse. Together they let you understand, test, change and reuse each module in isolation instead of reasoning about the whole system.

recall.q: Why are globals and control flags harmful? Give the fix for each.
recall.a: Globals let any module change shared state invisibly, so faults are untraceable; fix with parameters and return values. Control flags merge two behaviours into one function with extra caller coupling; fix by splitting into two functions.

recall.q: When should duplicated code be consolidated, and when not?
recall.a: Consolidate genuinely identical tasks (keep one copy, extract the shared core) because copies multiply testing and fix costs. Do not force reuse of merely similar tasks or let it damage cohesion; the coupling cost must be worth it.

citations.excerpt: Design sits between requirements and code. Modularity means self-contained modules with one job; Lehman laws demand continuing change while fighting increasing complexity. Aim for high cohesion, low coupling, information hiding and reuse; maintenance (corrective, perfective, adaptive) starts at delivery.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 16-45 (Coupling; calls; globals; control flags)
citations.excerpt: Coupling is dependence between modules; some is essential. Globals create hidden connections across all modules and should become parameters and return values. Long parameter lists signal multiple jobs; control flags such as isDate should split into separate functions.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 46-70 (Cohesion; relatedness; redundancy; reuse tradeoff)
citations.excerpt: Cohesion is focus within a module; split sequential tasks and unrelated validations. Duplicated code multiplies test and fix costs, unlike hardware redundancy, so consolidate shared cores such as calcXY; reuse only truly identical tasks since reuse adds coupling.

questions.prompt: Explain the four places Git work flows through and the commands that move work between them.

answer.text: Working directory (edit), staging area (git add stages), local repository (git commit snapshots), remote repository (git push shares, git pull/git clone collect). git status/diff/log inspect; git checkout/restore discard.
rubric: All four places named with roles

questions.prompt: Contrast local, centralised and distributed version control, and state which class Git belongs to with one reason teams prefer it.

answer.text: Local keeps history on one machine; centralised on one server (single point of failure); distributed gives every clone full history. Git is distributed: offline commits and no single failure point repay the need for branching discipline.

questions.prompt: Describe the safe team branching workflow and what happens when two branches edit the same lines.

answer.text: Feature branch off main, small logical commits, push, pull request, review, merge to main, everyone pulls; never commit on main directly. Same-line edits on both sides cause a merge conflict for a human to resolve.

questions.prompt: Define coupling and cohesion, and explain why fixing one often fixes the other.

answer.text: Coupling is dependence between modules; cohesion is focus within a module. Splitting an unfocused module removes the coupling its extra duties required, and decoupling forces each piece toward a single job.

questions.prompt: A function takes eight parameters including a Boolean mode flag. Name the two smells, explain the harm, and refactor.

answer.text: Long parameter list (doing several jobs; callers carry context) plus control flag (two behaviours, caller knows internals). Split by job and by flag: e.g. formatTimeDate becomes formatDate(day,month,year) plus formatTime(hr,min,sec) with grouped data.

questions.prompt: When should duplicated code be consolidated, and when should reuse be refused? Illustrate with the calcXY example.

answer.text: Consolidate genuinely identical fragments (extract calcXY shared by printSpecial and getNM) since copies multiply testing and missed fixes. Refuse when tasks are merely similar or merging harms cohesion, because reuse adds coupling.
